Candas Jane Dorsey is an internationally-known, award-winning author, editor, commentator, teacher of writing and communications, freelancer and cultural industries founder, community-builder, advocate, and arts community lifer.

She has written thirteen and a half books and counting. Her novels include multiple-award-winner Black Wine (originally Tor 1997, 1998, re-released Five Rivers 2013); Paradigm of Earth (2001, 2002, Tor); upcoming mystery series The Adventures of Isabel, What’s the Matter with Mary Jane? and He Wasn’t There Again Today (ECW, 2020-2022); upcoming YA novel The Story of My Life, Ongoing, by C.J.Cobb [working title] (Inanna, 2021), and International 3-Day Novel-Writing Competition winner (co-written with Nora Abercrombie) Hardwired Angel (Pulp Press 1986, optioned for film 1996.)

Her short story collections include the groundbreaking Machine Sex and other stories (Tesseract,1988, including the Aurora-Award-winning story “Sleeping in a Box”), Dark Earth Dreams(A Tesseract/Phoenix Discbook, 1994, audiobook with musical score), Vanilla and other stories (NeWest, 2000) and ICE and other stories (PS Publishing, 2018).

She is also author of five poetry books: this is for you, Orion rising, and Results of the Ring Toss from bill bissett’s blewointmentpress 1973, 1974 and 1976; Leaving Marks (River Books 1992), and talking to the dead (a.k.a. meateaters and other relatives), under submission.
She has edited or co-edited several anthologies: Tesseracts3 (with Gerry Truscott), Prairie Fire WorldCon anthology edition, LandSpace (with Judy McCrosky), and Tesseracts8 (with John Clute).

Dorsey is known for her extensive formative work in the speculative writing community, particularly in Canada. Over her career of nearly 50 years, she has had numerous published stories, poems, reviews, and critical essays. She was editor/publisher fourteen years of literary press The Books Collective, including River Books and, for a time, Tesseract Books. She teaches writing to adults and youth, professional communications at MacEwan University, and speaks widely on SF and other topics. She was a major motivator and founding president of SFCanada, and has been president of the Writers Guild of Alberta.

In addition to being awarded numerous grants to develop her work, Dorsey has received a variety of awards and honours for her novels and short fiction. In addition, in 2005 she was awarded the Province of Alberta Centennial Gold Medal for her artistic achievement and community work, and in 2017 the WGA Golden Pen Award for Lifetime Achievement in the Literary Arts. She was inducted into the Canadian Science Fiction and Fantasy Hall of Fame in 2018, and the Edmonton Arts and Cultural Hall of Fame in 2019. Other awards include YWCA Woman of the Year Arts and Culture (1988), and an Edmonton Arts Achievement Award (1988). She is also a community activist, advocate and leader who has won two human rights awards and has served on many community boards and committees, community-building for neighbourhoods, heritage, social planning and human rights advocacy.

She was born as patient number 1768 in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, and lives in inner city Edmonton with her partner, the writer/performer Timothy J. Anderson, and two Pomeranians who will likely appear throughout this website, to improve its cuteness quotient.

Candas Jane Dorsey is a founding partner of Wooden Door & Associates, a professional communications company established in 1991. She has worked as a freelance writer and editor since 1979, as a communications consultant and analyst, and as a Public Affairs Officer with the Government of Alberta (1984–85), and she edited and managed the monthly arts newspaper The Edmonton Bullet from 1983 to 1988.

Her freelance work includes major projects involving community consultation, research and recommendations; magazine and newspaper journalism; editing and production of books, reports, courses and manuals; educational documents, course design and educational media scripts (for ACCESS Alberta, TVOntario and Mead Educational Media, among others); technical writing, software documentation and help-file architecture for clients including the City of Edmonton and Intuit Canada; brochures, speeches, news releases and other public information; document and book design; print, website and multimedia production coordinated with designers, photographers and artists; strategic plans; and consulting on communication needs. Reports she has written or substantively edited include Equal in Dignity and Rights, the Report of the Review Panel on the Alberta Human Rights Commission, and Children’s Interactive Television in Canada: a Feasibility Study.

Dorsey has taught writing and writing-related courses, workshops and intensives for schools, colleges, universities and continuing education venues since 1983. She is a sessional instructor in the Faculty of Communication Studies at MacEwan University and teaches for University of Alberta Extension and Metro Continuing Education; past venues include the Banff Centre and Clarion West, and she wrote the course Writing Speculative Fiction (ENGL 387) for Athabasca University. She holds a B.A. (with distinction) from the University of Alberta, a B.S.W. from the University of Calgary and an M.F.A. in Creative Writing from the University of British Columbia.
Other things I do, and links I like.

Candas Jane Dorsey was the founding president of SF Canada (1991–94) and served on Writers’ Guild of Alberta committees from 1982 to 1991 and on its executive from 1991 to 1994, as vice-president (1992–93) and president (1993–94). She was a founding member of The Books Collective (1992–2006), publisher and editor of its River Books and Tesseract Books imprints. A long-time community developer in the arts and in social advocacy, she is a board member of the Boyle Street Community League and has served on the boards of the Edmonton Social Planning Council and Edmonton Heritage Council, the Boyle Renaissance Advisory Committee, the Edmonton Police Service LGBTQ Liaison Committee (1994–2011) and Chief’s Advisory Committee on Hate and Bias Crime (2004–2011), and Friends of McDougall. She ran for Edmonton City Council in 2012.

title: Let us reflect upon soap.
excerpt: tl;dr: Soap. Spoiler Warning: Outcomes involving soap will be revealed. So, here’s a long story about soap. Before I can tell it I need to go back in history, as do those annoying recipe people on the…

children.text: tl;dr: Soap.
Spoiler Warning: Outcomes involving soap will be revealed.

So, here’s a long story about soap. Before I can tell it I need to go back in history, as do those annoying recipe people on the internet who won’t give you the damned recipe for bread pudding, they insist on telling you the whole story of four or five generations of bread-pudding makers in their family. I am going to tell you about soap and history.

Before I can tell that I will remind you of the well-known story of the woman who always cut an inch from the wide end of her huge roast hams before she put them in the roasting pan. “Why do you do that?” says her partner. “Because my mother always did,” she replies. So off they go to the mother, whose “why” was, “Because my mother always did.” Luckily, the grandmother was still on this side of the soil, and when asked why she cut an inch off her ham roasts, she said, “Because I never had a big enough pan.”
So you see, behaviours can persist without their reasons, down through generations.

So, soap. Now back in the day, soap was big deal. The following pocket history has been strained through my patience and outlook and may contain impurities, but it will still clean the window in the Way-Back Machine. Basically, soap was a thing the women and/or children and/or servants of the house made laboriously from things like saved animal fats and sifted fireplace ash (for the lye), with various scenting agents they grew themselves, and so on. Households had soap kettles, stirring paddles, soap moulds, and a general understanding of the preciousness of the finer grades of soap. “Fancy soap” came from specialty makers and were the stuff of legend, and gifts (birthday mostly, and holidays, I would assume, as giving soap for a courting gift would, it seems to me, have been presumptuous and insulting, all at once. But I have no citation for that, and apparently it was done, so what do I know?)

So then these bars of soap or buckets of soap were used for everything. Washing soap was shaved into tubs of boiling water. A sort of soap-jelly was ladled onto greasy pans for scrubbing. Face soap was carefully used to almost the last sliver.
But there came a moment when those slivers of soap were just too too thin. So then what?
Well, there was a jar. Or a small crock.

In the jar were the heels, as it were, of all the soap. The soap was covered with water, either once the jar was full or right from the get-go, depending on family habit. And that jar lived under the sink or in the pantry or wherever it was out of the way, until the housekeeping unit (I’m trying to be gender inclusive but let’s face it, it was the woman or women of the house, right?) decided one day to mush it all up into liquid soap again, so that it could be used up completely and thriftily (and all the labour to make it wouldn't be wasted).

This is all pretty smart, and had to have been going on for hundreds of years. But then come specialists, who start making commercial bars of soap. Eventually we end up with Pears. Or Dove. Or whatever (even Irish Spring, heaven help us). (And washing powder. And so on. But right now I am concerned with bar soap.) And now, what we have is soap that is purchased outside the house—but when it is used up to a sliver, it goes in a jar of water. Eventually, some liquid soap for beside the kitchen sink is made from it.

Then some more time goes by. The jar under the sink no longer has water in it. Sometimes it’s just an old plastic peanut butter container with a wide mouth (sometimes shaped like a bear... describing for a friend…) and it gets full of soap, but nothing happens. Another jar is added.

Now, I come from thrifty stock, and because I am a youngest child and was born when my mother was almost 37, and I am getting old(er), I have a direct line that is only two or three women back from 2020 to 1900. My great-grandmother, after whom I am named, was a settler in Alberta in 1904 when most of her twelve children, including my grandmother, were almost adults. I am sure Sarah Candas Smith Berry made her own soap—you can bet on it. She thought nothing of whipping up dinner for 24 on the spur of the moment, and according to my mother, “Willful waste makes woeful want” was something of a mantra of hers.

My grandmother Amanda Mae Berry was born in 1888. She married a storekeeper, so although they also farmed until retirement, I’m pretty sure she bought some of her soap. She and my grandfather were both from thrifty Scots Presbyterian stock, “salt of the Earth” they would say (though I wonder about that phrase a lot, as conquering armies used to salt the earth as they passed so that nothing would grow, but never mind that now), so Amanda Mae definitely would have turned the ends of the soap into liquid soap for kitchen use. They also conveyed a rigidly pragmatic set of life practices unto their five children, including my mother.

My mother was born at the end of 1915. The Great Depression shaped her childhood and thwarted her ambitions, but left her with an iron framework of habits and rules for households, work ethics, and life in general. You can take the girl out of the Scots Presbyterian Church, but you can’t take the Scots Presbyterian out of the girl. The ends of the soap Would Be Saved. We even knew why, and it is possible that during and after the war, when money was tight, she rendered those soap bits back into useable soap, but by the time I came along, the 1950s were spreading the Good News of disposable wealth, unlimited product, and a consumer’s responsibility to buy.

(Also gift soaps got a lot more varied, and Avon came along, but that’s a side rabbit hole I will try not to go down here, even though I still, in 2020, have some of those gift soaps, as by then they had become Too Nice to Use, leading to another necessary storage device on a different shelf, but Never Mind That Now!)

However, my mother was a stalwart who abided by tradition, and my father was careful and meticulous, and together they passed on to us the tradition of the soap-slivers jars. And I, despite what my mother sometimes had to say, was a dutiful daughter.

Also, in the meantime, to complicate the matter, I had learned a trick from a friend: If people are coming to stay, and you have just cleaned the bathroom and want it to look welcoming, put out a new bar of soap. It will make a huge subliminal difference. And it appears that this is so, but it creates a situation where soap-ends proliferate at about double the speed.

Every time I moved, I would look at this soap and speak the traditional words of letting go (“Oh, f*** it, I’m never going to make liquid soap!) and I would throw out anywhere from one to several containers-full.
But we have lived in this house for 18 years.

So normally I would be able to introduce you to a large stash of soap-heels—but sometime in the middle of winter (before COVID-19, so I have no excuse), I was cleaning out under the bathroom sink and I came upon several previously-hand-cream jars full of soap slivers, and an empty liquid soap pump-topped bottle. I then cleaned out the bathroom cupboard, and what surfaced but more ex-soap and another pump bottle?

At that moment, I had a Visitation from Beyond the Grave. The spirits of my ancestors came to me, and entered into me, and I thought of all this history, and I thought, “Maybe I should try that soap thing.”
tl;dr again: Dear Reader, I did.

I had a 9” tall wide-mothed plastic canister that I would otherwise have had to put in recycling. Such was the extent of my dutiful cleaving unto the tradition of generations that I could fill it about 3/4 of the way with a haphazard assortment of leftover soap slabs. I filled it to the top with water and tightened the lid, and shook it up a bit. Every now and again I would shake it again, and over the ensuing seven or eight months, the contents have devolved into a strange beige soup with small masses of mysterious white and ivory lurking in the depths like koi in a scholar’s green-tinted garden pond. (see left side of photo)

Another aside. Those who know me might think that the only thing domestic about me is that I live in a house, and to some degree it is true. But it is a house that retains many of the scaffolding techniques inherited from those people of iron, those generations of makers and keepers and recyclers and re-users. And I like my house, and despite occasional appearances to the contrary, I like it in order.

So it pleases me inordinately that as of this afternoon, beside both the bathroom and kitchen sinks sit re-used pump-topped hand soap bottles full of liquid soap, sufficiently soapy to do its job. And the container of dissolving soaps, which resembles sourdough starter in many ways, has been topped up to start creating the inevitably-necessary refills.
So—and thank you for waiting—here’s my mother’s recipe for bread pudding.
My mother Marie Dorsey’s Bread Pudding
Preheat oven to 350ºF. (We are pre-metric here. History is like that.)
In a deep (4+ inches), round 8- or 9-inch casserole dish, mix together:
either 2 or 3 eggs
¾ cup to 1 cup sugar
1 cup milk
Note: This isn’t about measuring-cup cooking. Use a coffee cup if you want, but not one of the big ones.

Cube and, if desired, butter all the leftover crusts and heels of bread you’ve saved in a bag in the fridge. If necessary, top up with enough sliced bread, cubed, to fill the dish to within 1 inch of top. (My family of origin would use white bread and white sugar and make a pale pudding, but darker breads and brown sugar will make a darker pudding.)
Add:
some raisins if desired (a handful or two, or a cup. You know, some.).
Stir perfunctorily.
Cover to top of bread contents with:
• some more milk. (You know. Some.)
Stir again if you feel like it. Or not.
Top with:
a liberal amount of cinnamon and a touch of nutmeg.

Bake in 350° oven for about one hour or microwave oven for approximately 10-12 minutes (time depends on the microwave). It is done when it rises, the top is slightly brown (in conventional oven), and when, if pudding is pricked with a wooden toothpick, toothpick emerges clean.
Putting a custard, caramel or chocolate sauce on top is daring and revisionist, but not a mortal sin.
Equally delicious served hot or cold.

Gluten-free note: If making with gluten-free bread, you probably will have to use the larger number of eggs for binding, even in the smaller sized dish. Gluten-free breads differ widely in composition, so consider your first attempt a test.

(p.s. BTW, this recipe will also appear in Food of My People, the anthology of food-related speculative fiction Ursula Pflug and I just edited and Exile Editions will be publishing sometime in 2021. And if you think that makes this post nothing but soft-soap and sawdur, well, you read to the end, didn’t you, so here we are together: wash your hands and have some bread pudding.)

title: crowdsourcing altruism in a small world
excerpt: “These are the days of miracle and wonder / and don’t cry baby don’t cry, don’t cry don’t cry” Paul Simon In these shut-in days of dodging a global pandemic, the world has become very small, and small…

children.text: “These are the days of miracle and wonder / and don’t cry baby don’t cry, don’t cry don’t cry” Paul Simon
In these shut-in days of dodging a global pandemic, the world has become very small, and small things have become larger:

This tiny bruise, for example, enlarged in the photo, is the site of a medical miracle: a radiologist and an x-ray technician made small talk while I watched on a screen as a needle struck slowly to my hip bone and deposited a load of cortisone. Now I can walk without crippling pain, for a few months anyway.

A hundred years ago, when the “Spanish flu” was ravaging the world, this routine procedure would have been science fiction. Now we have medical miracles of all sorts: eleven-minute cataract operations; knee and hip replacements, repaired retinas, invisible cleft palate repairs, body modifications.

If only all our social miracles kept pace with our physical ones. For my trans relatives and friends, I imagine a society where our shared social understanding of gender had kept pace with the physical means we have of altering it. There is absolutely no way of abstracting the medical struggle of trans people from the social context that rigidifies and codifies gender so profoundly that it is the first and last datum that accompanies us through our lives. There is absolutely no way of succeeding at the thought experiment of imaging our society without gender bullying. And this is both infuriating and annoying. Societies that did not have the medical miracles of hormones and sophisticated surgeries had to find other ways of accommodating the wide range and expression of gender, sometimes with success and sometimes not. Why are some people in the modern day choosing “not”? It is so much easier to be kind and altruistic.

Why do we sometimes default to social dysfunction so profound it is indistinguishable from stupidity? Why do we not always become, under social challenge, better than the norm instead of worse? In these days of miracle and wonder, why tend collectively to the petty, the petulant and the punitively xenophobic? But even more interesting, why sometimes do we do the right thing? Who was it who said he was more interested in why people do good that why we do evil?

The body politic is in the public eye as the pandemic sweeps the world, no respecter of rank or role. Countries with universal health care stand to fare better, and everyone is waiting for the US to implode. Their saviours may be unlikely altruists: sports franchises, usually generators of obscene profits, who instead shut down their operations fully in defense against our new plague, or breweries and perfumers turn to the making of hand sanitizer as a public service; or auto factories repurpose to build ventilators. Meanwhile governments, intended to serve the public good, instead, in America or Alberta, use the pandemic as a smoke screen to disguise pork-barreling and profiteering among corporate cronies. In Canada we still have public health care, but here in Alberta, it’s at risk as politicos look to Trumpian neo-fascism for their models of public service. Perhaps they are thinking of the other meaning of “service”.

Meanwhile, public health officials become social media and media heroes for their honesty and grace under terrible pressure, and the news machines are full of small, local, community miracles: big chain grocery stores raising the wages of frontline staff and making the first hour of the day seniors-only, for example.

Who’s running the altruism machine in these pandemic days? Apparently it’s crowd-sourced—and even more than that, apparently guided by a predominantly compassionate and intelligent crowd educating itself about “planking the curve”, staying home, washing our hands, taking care of each other.

Given the pathological level of public and governmental idiocy that we have been seeing over the last few years, this wave of altruism and good sense is astonishing. Some optimists are saying we will come out of this in a better state of humanity than we went in. They posit an inevitable, a breakthrough social miracle.

If it is, let it not be our last. Let’s catch up with our machines and medicines, and treat the dysfunctions of our world with the same sophistication, commitment, and change-willingness that we can treat our malfunctioning bodies.
Earlier draft: Contents, and Crowd-sourcing Altruism
This is a picture of a small miracle.
This is the enlargement of a tiny bruise. At its actual size, I can hide it with the very end of my little finger.

This bruise, with its central puncture-mark, is the result of a confluence of technologies and human understanding of medical science: the site of a deep injection of cortisone into my hip under digital x-ray guidance.

When I’m on a treatment table I ponder my contents. I’m not used to having contents. I’m used to thinking of myself as a kind of meat-marshmallow, or a special meaty kind of Pillsbury-dough shaped like a person*. I have a coastline, an infinite interface with the world, called my skin, and I really like the interface. But I’d prefer not to think about what’s inside there making the engine run.

I’m not one of those people who can slow their hearts down, or lift their soft (or is it hard?) palate on demand, or make their ears produce a thunder sound by clenching, or even wiggle my ears for the edification of babies. I’m dumb to the processes within unless they f*** me up, in which case I engage reluctantly and with some distaste

Maybe it’s some kind of atavistic response to hitherto-secret contents being visible, but I’m not that keen to see anyone else’s contents either. It’s why I didn’t have a medical career and retire with a pension.

But I do like looking at my interior when its visible via medical imaging, since I’m there anyway and it’s clean on a screen. I like seeing all those textbook snapshots of a hip joint’s bony knob, or a jaw bone in is socket, and realising it’s mine. I recognise my teeth in the x-ray of the skull beneath the skin. Then the tedious maintenance of an ageing body is alleviated by the astonishment whenever I deconstruct a process and talk with the awesome people charged with carrying it out.

Today in the live x-ray I watched my hip bone move in its joint, and once I held still, saw a needle go in and touch that bone, carrying a load of medication that will allow me to walk normally and without the pain and disability of bursitis for three months or so.

Today I noticed that digital x-ray imaging designed its sensor plates to preplace traditional x-ray plates in the same machines, so that only the computers, software and plate interface had to be updated: remarkably sane transitional thinking. I was treated with a matter-of-fact grace by the two medical people who oversaw and performed the process, one with her knowledge of her imaging machine and one with his knowledge of how to use what he saw on her screen to alleviate my pain. This is not just a thing that happens. It is choreographed.

One hundred years ago, this would have been science fiction—if anyone had even thought it was possible. Yet here we are. We can replace cataracts in 11 minutes and the patient can walk out of the building with nothing more than the lingering annoyance of eye-sedating and dilating drops that take time to wear off. When my mother was a nurse in 1938, cataract patients had to wait until they were fully blind, the surgery was fraught, and then they had to stay in bed for six weeks, not moving, with sandbags on either side of their heads, until healing was enough that they could safely go home. Today, a cataract patient puts on their sunglasses and calls a cab, and in Canada, in Alberta so far, it doesn’t cost if done in a public hospital.

If only our social miracles kept pace with our physical ones. I was thinking particularly today of trans relatives and friends, and imagining a society where our shared social understanding of gender had kept pace with the physical means we have of altering it. There is absolutely no way of abstracting the medical struggle of trans people from the social context that rigidifies and codifies gender so profoundly that it is the first and last datum that accompanies us through our lives. There is absolutely no way of succeeding at the thought experiment of imagining our society without gender bullying. And this is both infuriating and annoying.

Societies that did not have the medical miracles of hormones and sophisticated surgeries had to find other ways of accommodating the wide range and expression of gender, sometimes with success and sometimes not. Unfortunately, “not” usually won throughout history.

And why is that? Why do we default to social dysfunction so profound it is indistinguishable from stupidity? Why do we not become, under social challenge, better than the norm instead of worse? In these days of miracle and wonder, why do we default collectively to the petty, the petulant and the punitively xenophobic?

And yet, last week I was astonished in a positive way by the reaction to COVID-19 by major sports corporations. These multimillionaires and billionaires, who make a lot of money from sport, and employ a huge wodge of athletes, support staff, administration and logistical workers (arena staff, etc.), in response to a single player testing positive, and with a time lag measured in minutes, consulted the knowledgeable scientists, then stood up and without pomp or dithering, and did the right thing. Likewise and on the other end of the economic scale, precariously-funded arts organisations cancelled concerts, exhibits and launches, out of a need to do the right thing, and before they were officially shut down by government. While certain presidents south of the border and premiers north of it (not naming names, but I live in Alberta), have assumed self-serving positions, their public health officials and many people on the street are just going ahead, studying and consulting the fact-based evidence and the people who are gathering it, and doing what’s right.

Who’s running the altruism machine in these pandemic days? Apparently it’s crowd-sourced—and even more than that, apparently by a compassionate and intelligent crowd which is educating itself about the basic issues: the need to “lower the curve”, the need to stay home and wash our hands, the need to take care of the vulnerable.
Given the pathological level of public and governmental idiocy that we have been seeing over the last few years, this astonishing wave of altruism and good sense is a revelation and a joy.
And perhaps, a breakthrough social miracle.
Let it not be our last. Let’s catch up with our machines and medicines, and treat the sick world with the same sophistication, commitment, and change-willingness that we can treat our bodies.
